citation.title: Does Regression Produce Representative Estimates of Causal Effects?

standing_assumptions:
The work is Aronow and Samii, ‘Does Regression Produce Representative Estimates of Causal Effects?’, American Journal of Political Science 60(1): 250–267 (2016). Printed p. 249 + N is PDF p. N; Appendices A, B and C are printed pp. 262–265 (PDF pp. 13–16). Every passage below was read from the page images. The official erratum (AJPS 61(2): 504, 2017) concerns printed pp. 258 and 260 only and touches no target.

[Sampling and data: section ‘Data, Potential Outcomes, and Causal Effects’, p. 252 (PDF p. 3)] “Suppose that we begin with a population of interest and draw a sample indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, n$. We assume that the sample is self-weighting and representative—each member of the population has an equal probability of being selected. … All of the results in this article continue to apply if we substitute sampling from a fixed population with the super-population assumption. For all $i$ that appear in the sample, we measure (a) a causal factor of interest, or “treatment,” $D_i$, which may be continuous or binary; (b) a $K$-length row vector of control variables, $X_i$, that exhibit no perfect colinearities or measurement error; and (c) an outcome, $Y_i$. The sampling or super-population assumption implies that $D_i$, $X_i$, and $Y_i$ are random variables, although not necessarily independent.”

[Potential outcomes: p. 252 (PDF p. 3)] “for every potential value of $D_i$, each unit $i$ is assumed to possess a well-defined response. Thus, if $D_i$ can take on the values $d_1, d_2, \ldots$, then unit $i$’s potential outcomes are given by the corresponding values $Y_i(d_1), Y_i(d_2), \ldots$.”

[Expression (1): p. 253 (PDF p. 4)] “we suppose that potential outcomes take the following form: $Y_i(d) = Y_i(0) + \tau_i \cdot d$, (1) where $\tau_i$ is the causal effect for unit $i$ and $d$ is an arbitrary value of $D_i$. When the treatment is binary, $D_i \in \{0, 1\}$, then this characterization is completely general.”

[Expression (2): p. 253 (PDF p. 4)] “we assume that the control variables in $X_i$ are indeed sufficient for removing any confounding in the relationship between $D_i$ on $Y_i$, so that $(Y_i(0), \tau_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i | X_i$. (2)”

[Expression (3): p. 253 (PDF p. 4)] “We also assume that the conditional expected value of $D_i$ can be represented as a linear combination of the covariates in $X_i$. … Formally, this assumption may be written as $\mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i] = V_i\omega$, (3) where $V_i = (1 \quad X_i)$, $\omega$ is a $K + 1$ column vector of coefficients, and $\mathrm{E}[.]$ averages over the units in the population.”

[Expression (4): p. 254 (PDF p. 5)] “The goal is to estimate the average causal effect for the population. This is simply the expected value of the unit-level causal effects: $\bar\tau = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{Y_i(d') - Y_i(d)}{d' - d}\right]$, (4) where $d' \neq d$ are two arbitrary values that are possible for $D_i$.”

[Regression: section ‘Ordinary Least Squares Regression’, p. 254 (PDF p. 5)] “$Y_i = \alpha + \beta D_i + X_i\gamma + \epsilon_i$, (6) where $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ are model coefficients and $\epsilon_i$ is an error term. … We fit Model (6) using OLS to obtain estimates of the parameters, $\hat\alpha$, $\hat\beta$, and $\hat\gamma$. The estimate $\hat\beta$ is our regression estimate of the causal effect of $D_i$.”

[Expression (7) and the weight: p. 254 (PDF p. 5)] “$\hat\beta \overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]}$, where $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$. (7) We call $w_i$ the multiple regression weight for unit $i$. The relation $\overset{p}{\to}$ refers to convergence in probability as the sample size, $n$, gets larger and larger”.

[Effective sample and estimated weights: section ‘The Effective Sample from Ordinary Least Squares Regression’, p. 255 (PDF p. 6)] “Expression (7) implies that the effective sample is given by reweighting the original sample by the multiple regression weights—the $w_i$s. We may estimate each of the multiple regression weights with the estimator $\hat w_i = \tilde D_i^2$, where $\tilde D_i$ is the residual from a regression of $D_i$ on $X_i$.”

[Appendix A notation: p. 262 (PDF p. 13)] “Define $W_i = (1 \quad D_i \quad X_i)$, a $K + 2$-length row vector combining the constant, causal factor, and control variables, and $\delta = (\alpha \quad \beta \quad \gamma)'$, a $K + 2$-length column vector containing the model coefficients. Define the stacked matrix of regressors and outcome vector as $\mathbf{W} = \begin{pmatrix} W_1 \\ \vdots \\ W_n \end{pmatrix}$ and $Y = \begin{pmatrix} Y_1 \\ \vdots \\ Y_n \end{pmatrix}$. The OLS estimates may be written as $\begin{pmatrix} \hat\alpha \\ \hat\beta \\ \hat\gamma_1 \\ \vdots \\ \hat\gamma_k \end{pmatrix} = (\mathbf{W}'\mathbf{W})^{-1}\mathbf{W}'Y$. By partial regression, $\hat\beta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2}$, (12) where $\tilde D_i = D_i - V_i\hat\omega$, with $\mathbf{V} = (V_1' \quad \cdots \quad V_n')'$, $D = (D_1 \quad \cdots \quad D_n)'$, and $\hat\omega = (\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{V})^{-1}\mathbf{V}'D$.” (The last subscript of the coefficient column is printed $k$; the dimension is $K$: finding P015-N004.) Theorem A.1 writes the baseline outcome as $Y_{0i}$, the same object as $Y_i(0)$.

[General model of the section ‘Estimating Representative Causal Effects’: p. 260 (PDF p. 11)] “we now drop the assumption of local linearity, as stated by Expression (1). We instead define causal effects over arbitrary potential outcomes: $\tau_i(d, d') = \frac{Y_i(d') - Y_i(d)}{d' - d}$, where the $d$ and $d'$ in parentheses are to emphasize that causal effects are defined for treatment values $d$ and $d'$. … we continue to assume that $X_i$ is sufficient to control for all sources confounding between $D_i$ and outcomes that would be realized under treatments $d$ or $d'$. This is expressed formally as $(Y_i(d), Y_i(d')) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|X_i$. (11) Additionally, we no longer need to assume that the conditional expectation of $D_i$ is linear in the covariates.”

[Positivity: pp. 260–261 (PDF pp. 11–12)] “Positivity, loosely speaking, requires that, for all values of $X_i$ that appear in the target population, there is some probability of observing different values of $D_i$. … Formally, the positivity assumption is as follows: $\Pr[D_i = d|X_i = x] > 0, \quad \Pr[D_i = d'|X_i = x] > 0$ for all values of $x$ in the target population represented by the nominal sample. Given unconfoundedness and positivity, the average causal effect for the target population is defined by $\bar\tau(d, d') = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i(d, d')] = \frac{\mathrm{E}[Y_i(d')] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i(d)]}{d' - d}$. Expectations ($\mathrm{E}[.]$) are taken with respect to the target population.”

[Appendix C notation: p. 265 (PDF p. 16)] “$\Pr[Y_i = 1|D_i, X_i] = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_\ell + \beta_\ell D_i + X_i\gamma_\ell)$, where $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) = [1 + \exp(-a)]^{-1}$. We fit the model via maximum likelihood (ML) to obtain the coefficient vector, $\hat\theta = (\hat\alpha_\ell \quad \hat\beta_\ell \quad \hat\gamma_\ell)'$. As before, let $W_i = (1 \quad D_i \quad X_i)$. … $\mathrm{logit}(P_Y) = \log[P_Y/(1 - P_Y)]$, where $P_Y = \Pr[Y_i = 1]$”.

[Reading used by the targets; not printed] The units $(X_i, D_i, Y_i(\cdot))$ are treated as independent draws from one distribution (the super-population reading the paper allows on p. 252), and $\mathrm{E}[.]$, $\Pr[.]$, $\mathrm{Var}[.]$ refer to that distribution. The population form of the effective sample is the reweighted law $Q(A) = \mathrm{E}[w_i\mathbf{1}_A]/\mathrm{E}[w_i]$, defined when $0 < \mathrm{E}[w_i] < \infty$; its mean of a covariate is $\mu(Z_i) = \mathrm{E}[w_iZ_i]/\mathrm{E}[w_i]$, as in Expression (9). Condition 4 of Theorem A.1 (“The data are well behaved such that the OLS solutions converge to a limit”) is read as the moment, law-of-large-numbers and nonsingularity conditions that the proof on pp. 262–263 uses (finding P015-A001, not confirmed as an error).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: p. 257: ‘We can obtain an approximation of arbitrary precision for the weights by using a Taylor expansion of the inverse link function’, as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 257 (PDF p. 8), left column; the expansion point is also in Appendix C, p. 265 (PDF p. 16)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed claim: p. 257 (PDF p. 8)] “We can obtain an approximation of arbitrary precision for the weights by using a Taylor expansion of the inverse link function, $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(.)$. Suppose we center such an expansion on the logit of the mean of $Y_i$.” [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $f(a) = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) = 1/(1 + e^{-a})$ and let $T_N$ be the Taylor polynomial of $f$ of degree $N$ at $0$. Data: $200$ binary observations with regressors $(1, D)$ and no controls; the $100$ observations with $D = 0$ have one $Y = 1$, and the $100$ observations with $D = 1$ have ninety-nine $Y = 1$. Then: (a) the logistic log likelihood has the unique maximizer $\hat\alpha = -L$, $\hat\beta = 2L$ with $L = \log 99$; the fitted linear predictors are $-L$ and $L$ and the fitted probabilities are $f(-L) = 1/100$ and $f(L) = 99/100$; the design has full rank and both outcomes occur in both cells. (b) The mean of $Y$ is $1/2$, so the expansion point is $\mathrm{logit}(1/2) = 0$. (c) $L > 9/2 > \pi$, and $\pi$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series of $f$ at $0$. (d) For every degree $N \ge 0$, $|T_N(L) - f(L)| \ge \frac{49}{100}$ and $|T_N(-L) - f(-L)| \ge \frac{49}{100}$. (e) Consequently the treatment coordinate of the estimating equation at the maximum likelihood estimate, with $T_N$ substituted for $f$, is $S_{D,N} = 100\{99/100 - T_N(L)\}$ with $|S_{D,N}| \ge 49$ for every $N$, whereas the exact logistic score is $0$. No order of the Taylor expansion at the stated center approximates the fitted probabilities, hence the weights, to arbitrary precision.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) = 1/[1 + \exp(-a)]$ (p. 257, PDF p. 8) and the logistic model and estimating equation of Appendix C (p. 265, PDF p. 16; transcribed in the standing assumptions). ‘Taylor expansion … center[ed] on the logit of the mean of $Y_i$’: the Taylor polynomials of $f$ at $\mathrm{logit}(P_Y)$, where $P_Y$ is the mean of $Y$ (p. 257 and Appendix C, p. 265). The ‘weights’ of a logistic regression are not defined in the paper except through this expansion; the counterexample bounds the error of the expanded mean function at the fitted predictors, which is what any such approximation of the weights uses.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The validator's steps: $e < 11743/4320 < 11/4$ and $(11/4)^9 = 2357947691/262144 < 9801 = 99^2$, so $e^9 < 99^2$ and $L = \log 99 > 9/2$; $\pi < 4$. $f(z) = \frac12 + \sum_{k \ge 1} (-1)^{k-1}b_kz^{2k-1}$ with $b_k > 0$, $b_1 = 1/4$, $b_2 = 1/48$ and $b_{k+1}/b_k \ge 1/12$ for all $k \ge 1$ (log-convexity of $b_k = 2\sum_{j \ge 0}((2j+1)\pi)^{-2k}$). For real $a \ge 9/2$ the terms $t_k = b_ka^{2k-1}$ increase strictly, so the polynomial $P_k(a) = \frac12 + \sum_{j=1}^k (-1)^{j-1}t_j$ (which is $T_{2k-1} = T_{2k}$) satisfies $P_k(a) \ge \frac12 + \frac{a}{4} \ge \frac{13}{8}$ for odd $k$ and $P_k(a) \le \frac12 + \frac{a}{4} - \frac{a^3}{48} \le -\frac{35}{128}$ for even $k \ge 2$; $T_0 = 1/2$. Hence the errors at $L$ exceed $127/200$ (odd $k$), exceed $4043/3200$ (even $k$) and equal $49/100$ ($N = 0$). The bounds at $-L$ follow from $T_N(-a) = 1 - T_N(a)$ and $f(-a) = 1 - f(a)$.
canonical_claim.note: P015-E009 is rated an error, Minor. From derivation.md, sections 2–5 (exact checks in check.py; grouped data in grouped-data.csv). Part (d) for all $N$ rests on the partial-fraction expansion of $\tanh$, which may be costly to formalize; if so, state (d) in full and prove (a)–(c) and (d) for the degrees that can be reached, recording the status. A 400-observation variant with a binary control has the same failure. Not established: that approximations with other centers or other polynomial families fail, or that the first-order approximation is useless for small predictor deviations; the paper derives and uses only the first-order step, which stands.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Expression (7) and the sentence that introduces it, corrected (Conditions (1)–(3)); the OLS coefficient column of Appendix A, corrected ($\hat\gamma_K$)
canonical_claim.location: p. 254 (PDF p. 5), right column; Appendix A, p. 262 (PDF p. 13)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed: p. 254 (PDF p. 5)] “Applying results from partial regression (Greene 2008, 27–29) along with Conditions (1) and (3), multiple regression generates a weighted average of causal effects of the form $\hat\beta \overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]}$, where $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$. (7)” [Printed: p. 262 (PDF p. 13)] “The OLS estimates may be written as $\begin{pmatrix} \hat\alpha \\ \hat\beta \\ \hat\gamma_1 \\ \vdots \\ \hat\gamma_k \end{pmatrix} = (\mathbf{W}'\mathbf{W})^{-1}\mathbf{W}'Y$.” [Corrected text, from Sol’s smallest repair] “Applying results from partial regression (Greene 2008, 27–29) along with Conditions (1)–(3), multiple regression generates a weighted average of causal effects of the form $\hat\beta \overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]}$, where $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$. (7)”; and $\begin{pmatrix} \hat\alpha \\ \hat\beta \\ \hat\gamma_1 \\ \vdots \\ \hat\gamma_K \end{pmatrix} = (\mathbf{W}'\mathbf{W})^{-1}\mathbf{W}'Y$, a column of length $K + 2$. [Formal content, with every hypothesis] Under (1) $Y_i(d) = Y_i(0) + \tau_i\cdot d$, (2) $(Y_i(0), \tau_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|X_i$ and (3) $\mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i] = V_i\omega$, and the regularity of condition 4 of Theorem A.1, the OLS coefficient $\hat\beta$ on $D_i$ in the regression (6) of $Y_i$ on $(1, D_i, X_i)$ satisfies $\hat\beta \overset{p}{\to} \mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i]/\mathrm{E}[w_i]$ as $n \to \infty$. Condition (2) is used twice, in the two population identities $\mathrm{E}[D_iY_i(0)|X_i] = \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i]\,\mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)|X_i]$ and $\mathrm{E}[(D_i - V_i\omega)\tau_i|X_i] = \mathrm{E}[D_i - V_i\omega|X_i]\,\mathrm{E}[\tau_i|X_i] = 0$; Conditions (1) and (3) alone do not give them.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Expressions (1), (2), (3), (6) and (7), $V_i$, $\omega$, $W_i$, $\mathbf{W}$ and $Y$ (pp. 253–254 and 262, PDF pp. 4–5 and 13; transcribed in the standing assumptions). The corrected statement is the statement of Theorem A.1 (p. 262, PDF p. 13), which lists unconfoundedness as its condition 1; see P015-T22.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The same as for Theorem A.1 (P015-T22): the partial-regression identity (12), the exact decomposition (13), and the two population identities quoted in the statement (the display labelled (15) and the unnumbered display after it, p. 263, PDF p. 14).
canonical_claim.note: P015-N004 is rated an error, Minor (verdict confirmed in part): the sentence before (7) cites Conditions (1) and (3) and omits unconfoundedness (2), which the proof on p. 263 uses twice; and the coefficient column prints $\hat\gamma_k$ for $\hat\gamma_K$. The corrected statement coincides mathematically with Theorem A.1, so one Lean statement serves this target and P015-T22; it is listed separately because the correction is to the main-text statement. The validator supplied no counterexample to the printed citation and none is listed. The other parts of P015-N004 (the skipped equation number (14) and ‘cumulative density functions’ for distribution functions, p. 256) are not mathematical statements and are not targets.

canonical_claim.location: p. 262 (PDF p. 13); proof on pp. 262–263 (PDF pp. 13–14); main-text form, Expression (7), on p. 254 (PDF p. 5)
canonical_claim.statement: Theorem A.1. Given the data-generating process outlined in the main text, namely, that the following hold: 1. (Unconfoundedness) $(Y_i(0), \tau_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|X_i$. 2. (Locally linear unit-level effects) $Y_i = Y_{0i} + \tau_iD_i$. 3. (Linearity of treatment in control vector) $\mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i] = V_i\omega$, with $V_i = (1 \quad X_i)$ and $\omega$ a $K + 1$ column vector of coefficients. 4. The data are well behaved such that the OLS solutions converge to a limit. Then as $n \to \infty$, the OLS estimate $\hat\beta$ for the coefficient $\beta$ in Expression (6) obeys $\hat\beta \overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]}$, where $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The sample, $D_i$, $X_i$, $Y_i$, potential outcomes, Expressions (1)–(4), the regression (6), $\hat\beta$, $w_i$, and the Appendix A notation $W_i$, $\mathbf{W}$, $Y$, $\mathbf{V}$, $\tilde D_i$, $\hat\omega$ are transcribed in the standing assumptions (pp. 252–254 and 262, PDF pp. 3–5 and 13). $Y_{0i}$ is $Y_i(0)$. Condition 4 is informal; a sufficient reading, from the batch validator: the units are independent draws from one distribution; the sample averages of $V_i'V_i$, $V_i'D_i$, $D_i^2$, $D_iY_{0i}$, $V_i'Y_{0i}$, $D_i^2\tau_i$, $V_i'D_i\tau_i$ and $V_i'V_i\tau_i$ converge in probability to their finite expectations; $\mathrm{E}[V_i'V_i]$ is nonsingular; and $0 < \mathrm{E}[w_i] < \infty$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact, for each $n$ with $\mathbf{W}'\mathbf{W}$ invertible (pp. 262–263, PDF pp. 13–14): (a) partial regression, (12): $\hat\beta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2}$ with $\tilde D_i = D_i - V_i\hat\omega$ and $\hat\omega = (\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{V})^{-1}\mathbf{V}'D$ (and $\sum_i \tilde D_i^2 > 0$, $\sum_i \tilde D_iV_i = 0$). (b) The decomposition (13): substituting $Y_i = Y_{0i} + \tau_iD_i$ and $D_i = \tilde D_i + V_i\hat\omega$, $\hat\beta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_iY_{0i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_iV_i\hat\omega\tau_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2\tau_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2}$. Population identities under conditions 1 and 3: (c) the display labelled (15): $\mathrm{E}[D_iY_{0i}] - \mathrm{E}[(V_i\omega)Y_{0i}] = \mathrm{E}_X[\mathrm{E}[D_iY_{0i}|X_i]] - \mathrm{E}_X[(V_i\omega)\mathrm{E}[Y_{0i}|X_i]] = \mathrm{E}_X[\mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i]\mathrm{E}[Y_{0i}|X_i]] - \mathrm{E}_X[(V_i\omega)\mathrm{E}[Y_{0i}|X_i]] = 0$; (d) $\mathrm{E}[(D_i - V_i\omega)V_i\omega\tau_i] = \mathrm{E}_X[V_i\omega\,\mathrm{E}[(D_i - V_i\omega)\tau_i|X_i]] = 0$; (e) Expression (8), $\mathrm{E}[w_i|X_i] = \mathrm{Var}[D_i|X_i]$ (P015-T19). Limits printed in the proof: $\hat\omega \overset{p}{\to} \omega$; $\frac1n\sum_i \tilde D_i^2 \overset{p}{\to} \mathrm{E}[w_i]$; first term $\overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[D_iY_{0i}] - \mathrm{E}[(V_i\omega)Y_{0i}]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]}$; second term $\overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[(D_i - V_i\omega)V_i\omega\tau_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]}$; third term $\frac{\sum_i (D_i - V_i\hat\omega)^2\tau_i}{\sum_i (D_i - V_i\hat\omega)^2} \overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]}$.
canonical_claim.note: The paper's main result (headline claim P015-H1; its main-text form is Expression (7)). Both readers followed the proof line by line and checked the limit against exact population OLS on discrete designs; it held up. The only confirmed finding that touches it is P015-N004 (Minor): the main-text sentence before (7) omits Condition (2) and the coefficient column prints $\hat\gamma_k$; the theorem itself lists unconfoundedness, so the corrected main-text statement (P015-T15) is this theorem. The allegation that condition 4 is too vague (P015-A001) was not confirmed; regularity-derivation.txt gives the sufficient moment and law-of-large-numbers reading quoted in definitions_needed, which the formalizer should make explicit as hypotheses and not weaken. The label (14) is skipped in the proof; the display after (13) is labelled (15). State the limit as convergence in probability and prove the finite lemmas (a)–(e).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Expression (9): the weighted mean of a covariate with the estimated weights converges to its effective-sample mean
canonical_claim.location: p. 255 (PDF p. 6), right column, continued on p. 256 (PDF p. 7)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed: pp. 255–256 (PDF pp. 6–7)] “Expression (7) implies that the effective sample is given by reweighting the original sample by the multiple regression weights—the $w_i$s. We may estimate each of the multiple regression weights with the estimator $\hat w_i = \tilde D_i^2$, where $\tilde D_i$ is the residual from a regression of $D_i$ on $X_i$. Then, much as we compute summary statistics for the nominal sample, we may use the multiple regression weights to estimate summary statistics for the effective sample. We can estimate the mean of a covariate $Z_i$ in the effective sample with $\hat\mu(Z_i) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \hat w_iZ_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \hat w_i} \overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[w_iZ_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]} = \mu(Z_i)$, (9) where $\mu(.)$ refers to the mean for the effective sample.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$ (Expression (7), p. 254, PDF p. 5); $\tilde D_i = D_i - V_i\hat\omega$ with $\hat\omega = (\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{V})^{-1}\mathbf{V}'D$ (Appendix A, p. 262, PDF p. 13); Expression (3), $\mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i] = V_i\omega$ (p. 253, PDF p. 4). $Z_i$ is a real covariate measured on unit $i$ (the paper's example, p. 256: an indicator for ‘unit is in Europe’). The paper states no regularity conditions for (9) and gives no proof; a sufficient reading, in the manner of condition 4 of Theorem A.1: independent draws from one distribution, Expression (3), $\mathrm{E}[V_i'V_i]$ nonsingular, $0 < \mathrm{E}[w_i] < \infty$, and convergence in probability to finite expectations of the sample averages of $V_i'V_i$, $V_i'D_i$, $w_iZ_i$, $w_i$, $(D_i - V_i\omega)Z_iV_i$, $(D_i - V_i\omega)V_i$, $Z_iV_i'V_i$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Not printed (the paper gives no proof of (9)); the exact identity on which the limit rests, for each $n$: since $\tilde D_i = (D_i - V_i\omega) - V_i(\hat\omega - \omega)$, $\frac1n\sum_i \hat w_iZ_i = \frac1n\sum_i w_iZ_i - 2\left[\frac1n\sum_i (D_i - V_i\omega)Z_iV_i\right](\hat\omega - \omega) + (\hat\omega - \omega)'\left[\frac1n\sum_i Z_iV_i'V_i\right](\hat\omega - \omega)$, and the same with $Z_i \equiv 1$ for the denominator. Also exact, on both of the paper's data sets and in general: $\sum_i \tilde D_iY_i/\sum_i \hat w_i = \hat\beta$ (Expression (12)).
canonical_claim.note: The formal part of headline claim P015-H2 (the effective sample can be studied by reweighting with the squared residuals). Both readers checked that (9) follows from $\hat\omega \overset{p}{\to} \omega$ and a law of large numbers; the formula held up. The reader's ‘problem found’ under this claim is the country-level implementation in the Jensen example (means in place of sums, P015-E001, Moderate), which is a finding about computed numbers with no mathematical statement to correct and is not a target. The regularity conditions in definitions_needed are this brief's sufficient reading and should appear as explicit hypotheses.

canonical_claim.location: p. 263 (PDF p. 14); main-text form in section ‘Randomized Experiments’, p. 256 (PDF p. 7)
canonical_claim.statement: Corollary A.1. Given the data-generating process outlined in the main text, if $D_i$ is randomly assigned, then as $n \to \infty$, $\hat\beta \overset{p}{\to} \bar\tau$. Proof. Under random assignment, $w_i \perp \tau_i$. Then, by random sampling and Slutsky’s theorem, $\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2\tau_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2} \overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[w_i]\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]} = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i] = \bar\tau$. □ [The hypothesis ‘randomly assigned’ as the main text states it: section ‘Randomized Experiments’, p. 256 (PDF p. 7)] “suppose that $D_i$ were randomly assigned, as would be the case in a well-executed randomized experiment with equal assignment probabilities. Then $D_i$ would be independent of $\tau_i$ as well as $X_i$, in which case $w_i$ would be independent of $\tau_i$. As a result, the weights in Expression (7) would effectively cancel out, and $\hat\beta$ would converge to $\bar\tau$. (See Corollary A.1 in the appendix.)”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for Theorem A.1 (P015-T22): Expressions (1), (4), (6), (7), $\tilde D_i$, and the reading of condition 4. ‘Randomly assigned’ is read, as on p. 256, as $D_i$ independent of $(Y_i(0), \tau_i, X_i)$ with one assignment distribution for all units (equal assignment probabilities); then Expression (2) holds, and Expression (3) holds with $\omega = (\mathrm{E}[D_i], 0, \ldots, 0)'$. Footnote 15 (p. 256, PDF p. 7) excludes designs with assignment probabilities that vary across units: for those the regression “will estimate a reweighted causal effect as in Expression (7)”.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact population facts on which the limit rests: if $D_i$ is independent of $(\tau_i, X_i)$ then $\mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i] = \mathrm{E}[D_i]$, so $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i])^2$ is a function of $D_i$ alone, hence independent of $\tau_i$, and $\mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i] = \mathrm{E}[w_i]\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$; with $\mathrm{E}[w_i] = \mathrm{Var}[D_i] > 0$, $\mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i]/\mathrm{E}[w_i] = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i] = \bar\tau$. The rest is Theorem A.1 (P015-T22) and its finite lemmas. For contrast (batch validator; consistent with footnote 15): with $\Pr[X=0] = \Pr[X=1] = 1/2$, $\Pr[D=1|X=0] = 4/5$, $\Pr[D=1|X=1] = 1/10$, $\tau = 0$ at $X = 0$ and $\tau = 2$ at $X = 1$, $\bar\tau = 1$ while $\mathrm{E}[w\tau]/\mathrm{E}[w] = 18/25$.
